articles.title: Where have all the buyers gone? DC homes lose value as demand dries up
articles.summary: News News: Washington’s housing market is sending an unusual signal: homes are available, sellers are cutting prices, but buyers are still not coming forward.Nea.
articles.body: Washington’s housing market is sending an unusual signal: homes are available, sellers are cutting prices, but buyers are still not coming forward.Nearly one in five homes listed for sale in the US capital is now priced below what its owner originally paid. At 17.8%, Washington has the highest share of such listings among the states and territories tracked by real estate analytics firm Parcl Labs. The national average is only 6.9%, as reported by the New York Post.The gap with other markets is striking. Colorado, which ranks second, has 11.8% of homes listed below their original purchase price, followed by Florida and Hawaii at 10.9% each and Arizona at 10%.The figures raise a bigger question for Washington’s housing market: Is the city running short of buyers?Why buyers are staying awayParcl Labs’ research suggests the immediate problem is weak demand rather than too many homes being built.In its August report, “Washington, DC: The Housing Correction Enters a New Phase”, the firm found that Washington’s downturn differs from the oversupply-driven problems seen in Sunbelt markets such as Florida and Texas.Prices across the District were down 1.6% year-over-year as of mid-August. Over the same period, prices across the broader DC metro area rose 3.6%, while the national market gained 3%.Sales have also failed to recover from the market’s peak. Transactions remain about 45% below their 2021 level.That weakness is particularly visible in parts of the city where condos make up a large share of the housing stock.Some neighbourhoods are losing value fastThe sharpest declines are concentrated in Downtown, Southwest and Southeast Washington.In the ZIP code covering the Southwest Waterfront, the Wharf and Buzzard Point, prices have fallen 11.5% year-over-year. That has wiped out nearly a third of the neighbourhood’s value since its 2024 peak.The Golden Triangle and Dupont Circle area has also suffered, with prices down 8.1%.Lower-priced properties are facing the most pressure. Among condos and townhouses priced below $500,000, 45% of listings have had their prices cut. Nearly 15% have been classified by Parcl Labs as “fire-sale” listings, around twice the rate seen in any other price band.The weakness points to a market where affordability alone is not bringing buyers back. Sellers are cutting prices, yet demand remains subdued.“DC has quickly shifted from a market where buyers felt pressure to act to one where sellers are competing for their attention,” Mark Rutstein of Compass, who has worked in the DC real estate market for nearly 25 years, told The Post.“We’re seeing fewer showings across the board, and with high interest rates, uncertainty around the federal workforce and significant pressure on the condo market, buyers have more leverage than they’ve had in years, although well-located single-family homes and parts of the higher-end market continue to hold up better.”Top end is still attracting buyersThe picture is not uniformly bleak across the District.While condo-heavy areas are struggling, some higher-end neighbourhoods have continued to record price gains. Foxhall and the Palisades in Northwest Washington have seen prices rise 4.6% year-over-year, while Brookland is up 5.5%.That creates a sharp divide within the same housing market: cheaper condos and townhouses are bearing much of the pain, while parts of the luxury market continue to hold up.Investors see an opportunityEven as traditional buyers remain hesitant, investors are increasing their presence in Washington’s housing market.Their share of home purchases has risen from 12.3% to 19.2% this year. Through July, investors bought 1,121 properties, compared with 840 sales, a net gain of 281 homes.The increased investor activity comes as sellers struggle to find buyers willing to meet their asking prices.Fewer homes en route There is another shift taking place in Washington’s housing market that could matter in the years ahead: new housing construction has fallen sharply.Housing permits authorised in the District have dropped 79% since 2022, falling from 7,705 units to 1,591 last year. The decline has been driven almost entirely by a pullback in multifamily construction.That means fewer new homes are expected to enter the market in the years ahead.For now, however, the central problem remains demand. Washington has homes for sale, sellers are cutting prices and some are accepting less than they originally paid. Yet sales remain far below their 2021 peak.The data does not establish that Washington is literally running out of residents. But it does show a housing market struggling to attract enough buyers, leaving sellers competing for the attention of a shrinking pool of willing purchasers.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: A German tourist took a 2,400-year-old piece of Ancient Olympia home in the 1960s; more than 50 years later, she returned it to the birthplace of the Olympic Games
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A young German tourist visiting the archeological site of Ancient Olympia in Greece in the 1960s took home a small piece of history: a shard of potter.
articles.body: A young German tourist visiting the archeological site of Ancient Olympia in Greece in the 1960s took home a small piece of history: a shard of pottery dating back some 2,400 years. She held on to the relic for decades — first as a travel souvenir, then as a personal reminder of a trip long ago. Decades later the now elderly woman reached out to Greek authorities to facilitate the return of the artifact to the birthplace of the Olympic Games. Her choice, reported by media outlets including NDTV and People, closes a silent chapter of guilt and restitution that spans generations, and underscores how even small objects can bear a heavy moral burden over a lifetime.A memento from the birthplace of the Olympic GamesAncient Olympia, in the western Peloponnese, is one of the world’s most important archeological sites. It housed the sanctuary of Zeus and the first Olympic Games, which began in 776 BC and lasted for more than a thousand years. The site is littered with fragments of temples, altars, statues and everyday objects that once belonged to athletes, priests and visitors who came from all over the Greek world.In the 1960s, tourism at Olympia was growing, but site management and security were not as strict as they are today. Visitors could often walk relatively freely among the ruins, and it was not uncommon for tourists to pick up small stones, shards of pottery or other fragments as souvenirs. For many, these objects felt like harmless mementos, tiny pieces of a vast landscape that would not be missed.A small shard with a long shadowThe German woman who took the fragment has not been publicly named in most reports. She was young at the time, travelling through Greece during a period when the country was under military rule and international tourism was expanding rapidly. At Olympia, she picked up a piece of ancient pottery, later estimated to be about 2,400 years old, and brought it back to Germany.For decades, the shard remained in her home, stored away or displayed as a curiosity. Over time, what may have felt like an innocent act in her youth began to weigh on her. Friends, family or her own reflections reportedly reminded her that the object did not belong to her. It was part of a protected archaeological site, a piece of Greece’s cultural heritage that should remain in its place of origin.The decision to return the relicIn her later years, the woman decided to make amends. She contacted Greek cultural authorities, explaining that she had taken the fragment as a tourist and now wished to return it, as per reports. Details of her initial outreach have not been fully disclosed, but the process involved coordination between German and Greek officials, as well as archaeologists and museum staff responsible for the Olympia site.Reports differ on whether the formal handover of the artifact to Greek officials took place in 2024 or 2025. The return was not considered a criminal proceeding but an act of voluntary restoration. Greek officials said the gesture was symbolically important, and reflected growing awareness among former tourists over the ethics of taking items from archeological sites.Why little things matterTo the casual observer, a small shard of pottery can seem a trivial thing. No gold statue, no complete vase, and maybe no lines of people at a museum. But for archeologists and heritage professionals, every fragment contains information. Pottery shards can tell us about daily life, trade, dating of layers at a site and movement of people and goods in the ancient world.When tourists remove objects from archaeological sites, they disrupt that record. Even a single shard taken out of context loses part of its scientific value. Over decades, the cumulative effect of many visitors taking small souvenirs can amount to a significant loss of material from a site. That is why modern heritage laws in Greece and most other countries strictly prohibit the removal of artifacts, no matter how small.A broader pattern of returnsThe German woman’s case is not unique. In recent years, museums, collectors and private individuals around the world have returned thousands of artifacts to their countries of origin. High-profile cases involve major museums repatriating looted antiquities to Italy, Greece, Egypt and other nations. Alongside these large-scale restitutions, there is a quieter stream of returns from private citizens who, often late in life, decide to send objects back to where they came from.Archaeological authorities in Greece have reported receiving letters and packages from tourists who admit to taking stones, shards or small objects from sites such as Olympia, Delphi, Knossos and the Acropolis. Many express regret and a desire to correct a mistake made decades earlier. While the objects themselves may be modest, the returns are welcomed as signs of respect for cultural heritage and international cooperation.How the relic was received in OlympiaWhen the fragment arrived in Greece, it was received by officials from the Greek Ministry of Culture and staff associated with the Olympia archaeological site. Archaeologists examined the object to confirm its age and origin. Based on media reports, it was identified as a piece of ancient pottery consistent with material found at Olympia and dated to around the 4th century BCE, roughly 2,400 years old.The fragment was then returned to the care of the site, where it will be stored with other archaeological materials from Olympia. It may or may not be displayed to the public, but its primary value now lies in being part of the documented collection from the sanctuary rather than a private keepsake in a foreign home.A personal tale with a public moralThe woman who returned the relic did it as a very personal act. She said she felt a guilt she had carried for a long time and a desire to set things right before she died. In statements relayed through authorities or media, she expressed hope that her return of the object would encourage others to think carefully about what they take from historical sites.Greek officials have used the story to reinforce a broader message to tourists. They emphasise that archaeological sites are not souvenir shops. Every stone, shard and fragment belongs to the host country and to humanity’s shared heritage. Taking even a small piece is not only illegal but also diminishes the integrity of the site for future generations.What this means for travellers todayThe case offers a clear lesson for anyone visiting historical or archaeological sites around the world. Today, heritage laws are very strict and enforcement has improved a lot since the 1960s. Cameras, site guards, signage and international agreements make it far riskier and less acceptable to remove objects from protected areas.Travellers are encouraged to:Take only photographs and leave only footprints at archaeological sites.Respect barriers, signs and instructions from site staff.Understand that even small objects are part of a larger historical record that should remain intact.If they or someone they know has an object taken in the past, consider contacting cultural authorities about possible return.Closing a decades-long chapterMore than half a century after a young tourist picked up a piece of ancient pottery at Olympia, that fragment has come home. The woman’s decision to return it does not erase the original act, but it does offer a form of closure for her and a small restoration of integrity for the site.In the end, the story is less about the shard itself and more about the changing relationship between tourists and heritage. It shows how attitudes develop over a lifetime, how one single act of restitution can send a message far beyond one person’s conscience. The homecoming of this tiny relic to Ancient Olympia, where the Olympic spirit was born, is a gentle reminder that respecting the past is a victory in itself.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Scientists found a strange golden coral deep beneath the Pacific; it was so different they created a new family for it
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Scientists exploring deep-sea mountains beneath the Pacific Ocean off Costa Rica have discovered a striking ‘golden coral’ so different from known spe.
articles.body: Scientists exploring deep-sea mountains beneath the Pacific Ocean off Costa Rica have discovered a striking ‘golden coral’ so different from known species that researchers created an entirely new family to classify it. The bright yellow, tree-like coral was found between 360 and 529 metres below the surface, growing on rocky outcrops covered with brittle stars. According to a study published in ‘ZooKeys,’ its physical features and genetic makeup made its position in the coral family tree difficult to establish. The researchers examined hundreds of genes to solve the mystery and confirmed that this coral represented a distinct evolutionary lineage. Named ‘Laurinque elenya,’ the species belongs to the newly created family Laurinqueidae. The discovery adds another piece to life in the deep ocean, where remote habitats continue to reveal species that have remained unknown to science.How did scientists find the unique golden coral deep beneath the Pacific off Costa RicaThe discovery emerged during scientific expeditions to underwater mountains, off Costa Rica in 2019 and 2023. These rocky environments lie far below the ocean surface and can support a variety of marine life. According to the study, researchers used the remotely operated vehicle ‘SuBastian’ to explore the seafloor and collect specimens. The vehicle was deployed during expeditions aboard the research vessels ‘Falkor and Falkor (too).’ The coral was found around ‘Isla del Coco’ and along Costa Rica's Pacific margin. Its bright yellow branches immediately distinguished it from the surrounding environment. Some colonies grew to more than a metre tall, rising from rocky surfaces densely covered with brittle stars. At that stage, however, the researchers did not know that the striking coral would eventually lead them to create a completely new family.How genetic evidence showed the golden coral belonged to a brand new familyIdentifying the coral's closest relatives proved more complicated than expected. According to the EurekAlert, scientists first sequenced three genes commonly used to study relationships between corals. Instead of providing a clear result, the genes linked the new coral to different and unrelated families. The researchers then adopted a broader genetic approach, examining hundreds of genes rather than relying on a small number of genetic markers.This analysis showed that the coral represented a separate lineage. It was closely related to the family Eunicellidae, but the researchers found enough differences in its genetics and anatomy to justify placing it in its own family. The study established ‘Laurinqueidae’ as a new family and ‘Laurinque’ as a new genus, with Laurinque elenya becoming the first described species within this newly recognised group. According to the study, genetic evidence and physical characteristics were important in demonstrating that the coral did not belong to an existing family.The scientific name reflects a remarkable deep-sea landscapeThe researchers drew inspiration from the coral's appearance and surroundings when choosing its name. According to the EurekAlert, Laurinque comes from ‘Laurinquë,’ a Quenya word meaning ‘golden tree.’ The name refers to the species' vivid yellow colour and branching shape. Meanwhile, the species name ‘elenya’ means stellar or ‘of the stars.’ It refers to the brittle stars that covered the seafloor around the coral colonies. The name therefore captures both the appearance of the coral and the unusual habitat in which it was discovered.The discovery highlights how much remains unknown within the oceansThe deep ocean remains one of the least explored environments on Earth, despite covering a vast part of the planet. According to the EurekAlert, research around Costa Rica's seamounts is continuing to document marine life that has not previously been known to science. Such discoveries can improve understanding of the biodiversity found in deep and difficult-to-reach habitats. The newly described coral also adds to knowledge of vulnerable marine ecosystems. Coral gardens create important habitats for other organisms, making the study of these environments valuable for understanding deep-sea life. Deep beneath the Pacific, a golden coral had remained unnoticed until modern exploration revealed that it represented not just a new species, but an entirely new branch of the coral family tree.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Who is Arthur Lundeen? Arizona man duct-taped to seat on American Airlines flight after alleged racist outburst
articles.summary: US News: The man whose photo on an American Airlines flight went viral as he was duct-taped to the seat by the crew and the other passengers has been identifie.
articles.body: The man whose photo on an American Airlines flight went viral as he was duct-taped to the seat by the crew and the other passengers has been identified as 67-year-old Arizonan Arthur Lundeen. He was arrested after an American Airlines flight from Dallas-Fort Worth to Newark was diverted to Baltimore when he allegedly became violent, hurled racist and anti-LGBTQ slurs, and attacked people on board. The video of how he was brought under control and the photos of Lundeen taped to the seat went viral.Lundeen was identified by Maryland Transportation Authority Police as the passenger at the centre of the September 3 incident aboard American Airlines Flight 618. The flight was travelling from Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport in Texas to Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey when the disturbance broke out.According to investigators and reports from passengers, the situation escalated roughly two hours into the flight. Lundeen allegedly began shouting profanities and racial and homophobic slurs. He reportedly directed an offensive racial slur at a Black flight attendant who attempted to intervene.The confrontation then allegedly turned physical. Lundeen was accused of striking the passenger sitting next to him and damaging the passenger's computer. A woman who tried to help was also allegedly pushed.With the situation escalating inside the aircraft, other passengers and members of the flight crew intervened. Lundeen's hands were restrained using zip ties, while duct tape was subsequently used to secure him to his seat.The aircraft was diverted to Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport, where police boarded the plane and arrested Lundeen after it landed.According to Maryland court records cited in reports, Lundeen is from Tucson, Arizona. He has been charged in Anne Arundel County, Maryland, with second-degree assault and disorderly conduct.'I would be scared if that person was on my flight'Passengers at Baltimore/Washington International Airport said they were shocked by the images. "That's crazy. I've never seen something like that. I would be scared if that person was on my flight," BWI passenger Kaunain Hashmi said. Another passenger, Jeff Vogel, said he had heard of unruly passengers being restrained on flights but had never experienced anything similar."Most of the flights I've been on have been pretty calm," Vogel said. "But I've heard of flights where people are quite unruly and they have had to restrain people with zip ties and tape and all sorts of things."Lundeen was released on bond on September 4, according to reports, and is scheduled to appear in court again on October 19.In a statement, American Airlines said the safety and security of its customers and team members is its top priority and that it does not tolerate violence."On Sept. 3, American Airlines flight 618 diverted to Baltimore (BWI) due to a disruptive customer. Upon arrival, law enforcement met the aircraft and assisted with deplaning the customer before the flight continued to its destination. The safety and security of our customers and team members is our top priority and we do not tolerate violence. We thank our team members for their professionalism and our customers for their understanding," said the airline.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: The freakout over data centers is just another fracking backlash we need to ignore
articles.summary: America's important fracking victory offers a blueprint for AI data center builders facing 70% public opposition and major Chinese competition.
articles.body: The future of America as a high-tech superpower is at a tipping point. The latest Fox poll shows 70% of Americans now oppose building new data centers in their communities, even though they are crucial to our future as a high-tech economy. Another report shows that 40% of new data centers have been delayed or canceled in 2026 — news that’s deeply welcome to our opponents in the artificial intelligence (AI) and tech race, the Communist Chinese Party. Data centers have become an electoral issue for the midterms, even in a red state like Texas where Republican Gov. Greg Abbott has announced a construction moratorium. It’s probably the only thing he has in common with ultra-liberal Democrat Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York: a willingness to hit the pause button on data centers. FROM NEW YORK TO TEXAS, STATES SHOULD RESPECT LOCAL CONTROL ON DATA CENTERS This backlash comes despite the fact that every policymaker knows that data centers are needed to power our future economy, from AI to the Internet of Things and the cloud, and that the only real beneficiary of a moratorium will be China. Still, the public remains unconvinced, especially when it faces a zoning proposal to build a data center half a mile from its backyard. This all sounds discouraging, but we’ve been here before. Just a decade ago, the advent of large-scale fracking, or horizontal drilling, for oil and gas faced a similar frenzy of opposition. If today’s anti-data center forces have strong support from communist China (which has been linked to more than 200 accounts on X, promoting data center misinformation) then it was Russian President Vladimir Putin’s Russian media that amplified the anti-fracking movement here and in Europe. FOX NEWS POLL: COOL YOUR SERVERS! VOTERS REJECT DATA CENTERS It got so bad that fracking became a flashpoint in the culture wars, with left-wing celebrities like Jane Fonda, Matt Damon and Mark Ruffalo organizing protests and blockades, resulting in bans on fracking in several states. Yet, in the end, the fearmongers lost and the energy companies won, as did America’s strategic and economic interests. Today, thanks to fracking, America is the world’s No. 1 oil and gas producer. That’s why hostilities with Iran haven’t caused a panic at the pump. A new report by the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston says without America’s current oil and gas independence, the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz would have cut the U.S. employment rate by nearly 2%. How the energy companies turned the public around on fracking offers powerful lessons for today’s AI executives and power companies on data centers. KEVIN O'LEARY WARNS CHINA IS WINNING THE AI RACE BECAUSE U.S. STATES ARE SLOWING DATA CENTER PRODUCTION First, fracking companies understood that all politics with environmental issues like this, is local. This isn’t a war you can macro-manage from the boardroom or Washington. Instead, it’s a series of wars that have to be fought state by state, district by district, even neighborhood by neighborhood. This means partnering with local businesses and local governments, to talk about how building a new data center expands jobs and opportunities for everyone, not just AI or tech companies. It also means seeking out places that will welcome a new data center for the same reasons, and using them as examples of how data centers can coexist with traditional communities and values. CHINESE BOT FARM CAUGHT RED-HANDED TRYING TO INFLUENCE HEATED AI DATA CENTER DEBATE Second, it means partnering with responsible environmental and citizen associations to emphasize how data center builders will be staying within agreed-upon safety and cost guidelines, such as President Donald Trump’s insistence that they come with their own power supply so as not to raise electricity rates. This partnership can work to dispel the myths being spread by the opposition. One of those myths that nearly stopped fracking was that it polluted the water supply. Companies were able to prove that fracking didn’t affect the water supply except where the water table was already low- and where engineers wouldn’t want to sink a well, anyway. ‘BACKWARDS AND POOR’: TRUMP ISSUES DIRE WARNING TO COMMUNITIES BLOCKING CRITICAL TECHNOLOGY Anti-data center fanatics spread similar falsehoods about data centers using up water, when in fact your average golf course consumes more. Likewise, companies can emphasize that technical and safety improvements take place every year. The data centers built five years ago will look like technological dinosaurs compared to the ones that are coming. Still, the public remains unconvinced, especially when it faces a zoning proposal to build a data center half a mile from its backyard. Third, don’t let up on the focus of what happens if we don’t. Fracking executives were able to remind people of what energy dependence looked like, with long gas lines and soaring prices. We can remind average Americans of the gains China will make, and the advantages we lose, if Beijing wins the data center wars. Do you really want the country that gave us COVID-19 deciding the future of AI? CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Finally, people need to realize new data centers aren’t just about growing AI. They’re essential to modern life, as the number of devices we use requires more and more power. The average U.S. household uses between 17 and 21 internet-connected devices, compared to only two or three devices in 2010. All that connectivity makes increasing demands the future grid won’t be able to match without new data centers. articles.title: US mom hanged 2-year-old son after discussing Lindsay Clancy case with friends, called him ‘anti-Christ’
articles.summary: US News: Corie Walsh, a 38-year-old mother, was charged with the first-degree murder of her 2-year-old son Barrett. The shocking incident occurred shortly after she discussed the Lindsay Clancy case, leading authorities to investigate her mental state and motivations.
articles.body: A US mother who allegedly killed her 2-year-old son had been discussing the high-profile Lindsay Clancy case with friends just hours before the child was found dead.Corie Walsh, 38, faces three counts of first-degree murder after her son Barrett, who was also known as “Bear”, was found hanging in the basement of the family home, FOX 32 reported.A neighbour discovered the boy with his feet off the ground and a ligature around his neck and called 911. The neighbour told emergency operators that Walsh had no pulse while CPR was being performed.Paramedics pronounced Barrett dead at the scene. An autopsy later determined that he died from asphyxiation.Police also found Walsh in a bathtub, fully clothed and in bloody water. She was taken to hospital after officers determined that she had attempted to harm herself. Her injuries were not considered life-threatening, according to the court proffer viewed by the outlet.Prosecutors allege Walsh later told investigators that she killed Barrett because she believed he was the “anti-Christ” and the “devil”. While she was receiving medical treatment, she also described how the killing allegedly occurred.The case has drawn attention to Walsh’s conversations about Clancy, a Massachusetts mother and nurse whose trial was underway when Barrett died. Clancy was accused of killing her three children before attempting suicide and argued that she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis. After more than 30 hours of deliberations over nearly seven days, the jury was unable to reach a unanimous verdict, and on Friday, the judge declared a mistrial.According to prosecutors, Walsh exchanged messages with friends about the Clancy case at about 12:30 pm on Tuesday, roughly three hours before Barrett was found.Walsh’s husband was out of town when the alleged killing occurred and returned home by plane later that evening.Walsh was taken to the hospital after the incident and will be transferred to the Will County Adult Detention Facility once she is medically cleared. articles.title: Putin orders 3-day pause in strikes against Kyiv as US delegation arrives in Russia
articles.summary: Europe News: Russian President Vladimir Putin has ordered Russian forces not to launch strikes against Kyiv for three days as US special representatives Steve Witk.
articles.body: Russian President Vladimir Putin has ordered Russian forces not to launch strikes against Kyiv for three days as US special representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visit Moscow for talks on the war in Ukraine, according to the Kremlin.Putin is due to hold talks with Witkoff and Kushner on Saturday, Russia’s state news agency TASS reported, citing Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov“Putin has ordered that no strikes be carried out against Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight today,” Peskov said.The Kremlin announced it will brief the media after the Russian leader's discussions with the US special representatives.The order to halt strikes on Kyiv was issued in connection with preparations for the arrival of the American delegation.US envoys arrive in MoscowWitkoff and Kushner landed in Moscow on Saturday for talks aimed at reviving efforts to end Russia’s war in Ukraine, which is now in its fifth year. Two people familiar with the visit told Reuters that the US envoys were met at the airport by Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev.A witness saw a motorcade carrying Witkoff, Kushner and Dmitriev leave Moscow’s governmental airport and head towards the city.Dmitriev has taken part in the US negotiators’ previous meetings with Putin and remained in contact with them during a pause in their visits to Russia.He also played a role in negotiating US sanction waivers for Russian oil this year.US President Donald Trump said on Friday that Washington had a fresh concrete proposal aimed at ending the war, but did not provide details.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Friday that Witkoff and Kushner would travel to Ukraine on Sunday after their Moscow visit.Kyiv attacks intensified before visitThe latest development comes after an escalation in long-range attacks by both Russia and Ukraine.Russian attacks killed five people in Ukraine overnight.Zelenskyy said Saturday that Ukraine would halt airstrikes during the US envoys’ visit and urged Moscow to do the same. Moscow had not publicly responded to that proposal before Putin’s order.Zelenskyy also said Russia had carried out overnight strikes on Kyiv and Boryspil international airports ahead of the planned US visit to Ukraine.“Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in a social media post.He added that Ukraine would adjust its operations regarding Russian airspace, which he said had become dangerous because of Ukrainian drones and missiles.A Russian drone also struck the headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service, the SBU, in Kyiv on Friday. The strike came during a period of heavy Russian attacks on the Ukrainian capital.Russia and Ukraine remain far apartThe US push to end the fighting has lost momentum, while Russia and Ukraine remain divided over the terms of a potential settlement.The Kremlin said on Friday that Putin’s position, set out in a speech two years ago, remained “unshakeable”. That position includes a demand that Ukraine cede the entire territory of four regions claimed by Russia and abandon its plan to join Nato.The front line, stretching about 1,250 kilometres (775 miles), has remained largely static, with Russia making gradual gains in its attempt to take the whole of Ukraine’s Donbas region.At the same time, both sides have intensified attacks deep inside each other’s territory since their last peace talks in February.Ukraine has targeted Russian oil refineries and other facilities with long-range drone strikes, while Russia has continued missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.The latest US diplomatic effort comes with Witkoff and Kushner expected to hold talks with Putin in Moscow on Saturday before travelling to Kyiv on Sunday.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2025, Michigan recycled more than 7,000 scrap tires into 0.8 miles of Ellsworth Road; the project later won a national green construction award
articles.summary: US News: What happens when thousands of worn-out tires reach the end of the road? In Michigan, some of them found their way back onto one. In 2025, more than 7.
articles.body: What happens when thousands of worn-out tires reach the end of the road? In Michigan, some of them found their way back onto one. In 2025, more than 7,000 scrap tires were recycled into rubber-modified asphalt used on approximately 0.8 miles of Ellsworth Road in Pittsfield Township. According to the Washtenaw County Road Commission (WCRC), the project was designed to test how pavement containing recycled tire rubber performs compared with conventional asphalt. The unusual road experiment brought together WCRC, Michigan Technological University and the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE) to explore a practical use for scrap tires while studying pavement performance.The experiment later received national recognition. In June 2026, EGLE announced that the Ellsworth Road project had received the National Asphalt Pavement Association's 2025 Quality in Construction Award - Green Category, recognising its use of recycled tire materials in pavement while pursuing sustainable infrastructure and pavement performance.Turning tires into roadsThe idea behind the project was straightforward: instead of allowing old vehicle tires to become waste, some of their rubber could be processed and incorporated into asphalt. Ellsworth Road, which runs between Platt Road and Carpenter Road in Pittsfield Township, was selected for the project in 2025. WCRC describes the work as a mill-and-resurfacing project, but it was different from an ordinary road resurfacing because researchers were using the project to evaluate rubber-modified asphalt made from scrap tires. The rubberised material was used on approximately 0.8 miles of Ellsworth Road, specifically between the bridge over I-94 and Carpenter Road. More than 7,000 scrap tires were designated for recycling into the rubber-modified asphalt used for that portion.The approach also allowed researchers to make a direct comparison. A separate section of Ellsworth Road, between Platt Road and the bridge over I-94, received traditional asphalt. By having conventional and rubber-modified pavement on different portions of the same road, researchers could observe how the two materials perform over time.Paving with recycled rubberThe construction work moved forward in August 2025. WCRC reported that Cadillac Asphalt, the project's contractor, completed paving Ellsworth Road on August 27. The agency specifically noted that the hot-mix asphalt used on designated sections included ground tire rubber. The purpose was not simply to dispose of old tires, but to study whether the modified material could offer improved durability and pavement performance. The project was funded through an EGLE grant and Michigan Transportation Funds. It brought together government agencies, researchers and industry partners to test a practical use for recycled tire material in transportation infrastructure. That distinction is important to the story. The tires were not simply placed underneath the road or used as a substitute for asphalt. Their rubber was incorporated into a rubberised hot-mix asphalt (RHMA) pavement mixture.Why recycled tires matterScrap tires can be difficult to manage when they reach the end of their useful life. Finding large-scale applications for recycled tire rubber can therefore create another market for a material that might otherwise become waste. According to EGLE, using RHMA can help conserve natural resources, reduce emissions and landfill waste, while also potentially improving pavement longevity. The agency described the Ellsworth Road project as the first road in the greater Ann Arbor area to incorporate this type of rubberised material. The project is also part of a wider effort in Michigan to find useful applications for scrap tires. EGLE said its Scrap Tire Program provides grants aimed at developing markets for scrap tires and expanding the use of rubberised asphalt in paving.From experiment to awardThe Ellsworth Road project gained another milestone after construction. In 2026, EGLE announced that the project had received the 2025 Quality in Construction Award - Green Category from the National Asphalt Pavement Association. The award recognised the innovative use of rubber-modified asphalt containing recycled tire materials and its combination of pavement performance goals with sustainable infrastructure.For Michigan, the recognition highlights how an everyday waste problem can be connected with road construction. Rather than treating worn-out tires only as a disposal challenge, the Ellsworth Road project tested whether their rubber could become part of a functioning transportation system. The results of the ongoing comparison between the rubber-modified and traditional pavement will help determine the approach's effectiveness over time. If the recycled-rubber pavement performs well, the project could provide useful evidence for considering similar applications elsewhere. The experiment on 0.8 miles of Ellsworth Road therefore represents more than a single resurfacing project. It is an effort to test whether thousands of discarded tires can be redirected from the waste stream and given another purpose, this time beneath the wheels of Michigan drivers.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: At 9.30 am on Aug 26, Laxmi Pandey rushed to the fourth floor of her mint-green family home with her 11-year-old daughter. Minutes before that, she was about to send little Pradisha off to school, but several people on the road told her that further up, the Trishuli river had flooded its banks and things didn't look good.Seven minutes later, the Trishuli roared in and ate up everything. Miraculously, it left Laxmi's mint-green house standing. Now, a little over a week from Aug 26, the 42-year-old and her family -- in-laws, husband, son and daughter -- are trying to stand up and face their uncertain fate. The house at Dhunge Bazar, in Nepal's Nuwakot district, survived the flood like a brick-and-mortar Noah's Ark, but the lives of the people it sheltered were altered forever. "It is hard," Laxmi confessed, then smiled and said: "Lekin darr ke aagey jeet hai (beyond fear lies victory)."Laxmi, who ran a liquor shop with her husband, Prakash Pyakurel (44), and father-in-law Chhata Bahadur Pyakurel (69), knows she can never go back to the house.The family will have to restart from scratch.Before the floodThe Trishuli river was the star of Nuwakot. Its water, gurgling down a narrow valley, made for a pretty picture. Chinese tourists from neighbouring Tibet passed through Dhunge Bazar. The place was also a halt for Kailash Mansarovar pilgrims, many of whom were Indian.They all stopped to stare at the river, which was a spot for picnics and pujas. As the town got decent tourist traffic, the Pyakurels' liquor store too got many kinds of visitors."This is the time of the year when people from other places come to take in the beautiful jharnas (waterfalls) that flow into the Trishuli," Laxmi said. "I also went to the jharnas whenever I found some free time."The mother of two, who co-ran the family trade and a household, had a busy life. "I used to wake up early, finish the household work and open the shop at 7.30 am. My husband used to reach the shop around 8.30 am. The whole day we managed supplies and interacted with customers. In the afternoon, my father-in-law used to be at the counter. The house was barely 5 minutes away from the shop," Laxmi said.The store, which was the only income stream for the family, vanished into the river before their eyes. Also gone were a car and a scooter."I had everything. Sab tha wahaan," Laxmi said. She paused, as if searching inside her own head a snapshot of herself from 10 days ago.Losing a communityIf the Nepal govt allowed and helped, would she go back to the house?"I can't go back, and the govt cannot do much either," Laxmi said. She explained why."In front of our house was a road. On the other side of the road were shanties. Now, all of that is a river. What can any govt do?" she asked.Going back to the house seems almost impossible for another reason. The raging river, in its wake, left deeper, but invisible, scars on the mind of the community."The family of seven that lived next door is missing. Woh sab beh gaye (they were swept away)," Laxmi said. There was no sorrow or shock in her voice or on her face. Those who survived the flood to tell the tale haven't just lost material possessions. They have lost an entire community, the very glue that binds all humans together. Dhunge Bazar, even if it is repopulated, will not be the same town.Laxmi and her family, though, have tried to preserve whatever little is left of the old human bonds in this new, uncertain life. When she moved to Kathmandu on Sept 3 to live in the accommodation of a well-wisher, Laxmi took another family in too. Sujan Tamang, who lost his house but braved the waters and rescued the Pyakurels, is the "bhai" Laxmi cannot stop talking about. "We are alive because of him. We got a second life. He came that very day and got us out through a window which had broken."When the river cameThe Pyakurel house has four floors, including the ground floor. There is also a small structure on the roof. "When the water entered, it went up three storeys. At one point, my daughter was waist-deep in the water on the third storey," Laxmi said. "Each wave felt like a force that was pushing to topple the house," she said. "With every thud, we thought this would be our last second. This is the end."At that time, all the family members were not at home. Laxmi's son, six-year-old Prayan Jang, was in school. "I was fretting about what would happen to him in school. My father-in-law said Prayan would be safe as the school is on higher ground." But this made Laxmi more worried. "I thought, if the river takes us all, and only my boy survives, what will happen to him? He will be alone."Fortunately, after their rescue, the family and the little boy were reunited. With the clothes they had on their backs, the Pyakurels waded out. A day after, Prakash and Laxmi went back to the house to see if anything could be salvaged. There was little left to take away. So, they too left the town and the river that had nurtured them for decades.The mint-green house, built 35 years ago by Chhata Bahadur, which became an internet sensation briefly, is now a brick-and-mortar shell."We can try to live somewhere close to the earlier house, but I just don't know what will happen," Laxmi said.Nature's rageIn the Indian sub-continent, many rivers, such as the Ganga and Yamuna, are worshipped as mothers. So also the Trishuli.Rivers are where people offer water to their ancestors, do their morning puja, and pray for their loved ones. Rivers are givers for the most part. The people of Nuwakot also knew the Trishuli river as a benign giver."When the first warning of the flood came, no one believed it. So no one tried to escape. My mother-in-law told me 'in all these years, the river has never breached its banks to enter the shanties. Kuchh nahin hoga (nothing terrible will happen)'," Laxmi said.So, when the river took everything, did it feel like the mother was pushing her children away?"Yes, it felt like that," Laxmi nodded. "But will I fight my mother? No, she is nature. I have to let her be."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In a first, 9 Isro staff bodies seek 'written clarity' on private sector shift
articles.summary: India News: BENGALURU: For the first time since the government began opening India’s space sector to private industry six years ago, nine employee bodies at Isro .
articles.body: BENGALURU: For the first time since the government began opening India’s space sector to private industry six years ago, nine employee bodies at Isro centres representing thousands of staff under the Department of Space (DoS), have formally raised concerns over the direction and basis of the transition. They have sought written clarification from chairman, space commission, who also serves as secretary, DoS and chairman, Isro.“Private participation in defined commercial activities can coexist with a strong, publicly owned Isro. What cannot be accepted without debate is a policy that reduces Isro to a residual R&D boutique while the realisation of the nation’s launch vehicles and the operation of its launch infrastructure pass out of public hands,” the representation dated Sept 4 and accessed by TOI, reads.Terming technology developed by Isro a national asset, they said its transfer must be transparent, accountable, and consistent with strategic, safety and employment considerations. “...Serving employees have an earned right to be informed, consulted and protected. Natural justice and good administration require that policy of this magnitude be explained to the workforce by the Department itself.”The joint representation has been signed by the Isro Staff Association, SHAR Employees Association, Isac Employees Association, Isro Staff Association-LPSC, Isro Staff Association-BBU, NRSA Employees Union, Space Employees Association-BBU, Isro Staff Association-IPRC and SAC Employees Welfare Association.Pointing to a recent public statement reportedly made by IN-SPACe chairman Pawan Goenka on Isro eventually “not manufacturing any launch vehicles”, they asked if his statement “represents an approved decision of the Govt of India, Space Commission or DoS… If approved, the date, authority and text of the policy decision may kindly be indicated.”“What will be the future mandated role of Isro — specifically, whether design, development, realisation, integration, testing and launch of PSLV, LVM-3, SSLV and successor vehicles will continue as Isro functions or will cease. Whether any decision has been taken to exclude PSUs from the proposed transfer of PSLV/LVM-3 production, and the justification for such exclusion,” they asked.They also sought in writing the institutional arrangement under which publicly created technology, test facilities, launch complexes and know-how — built with taxpayer funds and the labour of generations of Isro employees — are being transferred or opened to private operation, and the role of NSIL vis-a-vis IN-SPACe in such transfers.“Isro was built as a national scientific institution with public funds, public purpose and a public workforce. Launch-vehicle design, realisation, integration, testing and launch operations are not merely ‘manufacturing contracts’. They are the core competence, institutional memory and strategic capability of the organisation,” the representation reads.They said they have reasonable fear that a progressive withdrawal of Isro from launch-vehicle and satellite realisation will tamper experiments after research, shrink in-house work, freeze or reduce sanctioned strength, and close promotion and skill-development avenues in technical, scientific, administrative, stores, purchase, quality, safety and industrial cadres.“Existing employees may be rendered surplus, or redeployed, or left without meaningful work while the same tasks are performed by private contractors using publicly developed technology…Regular recruitment to Group A, B and C posts — already constrained by vacancies and attrition — will further decline, denying opportunity to meritorious youth who look to Isro as a public career of honour, not as a private contractor's workforce,” the letter reads.Congratulating Isro on the success of the GSLV-F17/EOS-05 mission, the letter read: “...We once again proved that we can rise from ashes and fly like a phoenix.”“We submit this in a constructive and democratic spirit. Our loyalty to Isro and to the national space programme isn’t in question. Precisely because of that loyalty, we consider it our duty to seek clarity before uncertainty hardens into irreversible policy,” they said, adding that they will plan further course of action once the written reply is received.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Jilted lover abducts girl's minor brother, drinks poison during 22-km police chase in Delhi
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A jilted lover who abducted a girl's 11-year-old brother and threatened to kill him unless she married him was hospitalised after consuming.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A jilted lover who abducted a girl's 11-year-old brother and threatened to kill him unless she married him was hospitalised after consuming poison during a 22-kilometre police chase here when cops were about to arrest him, police said on Saturday.Officials said the accused, Dharam Pal, a resident of Kasganj district in Uttar Pradesh, was immediately shifted to BJRM Hospital, where he remains in custody.The boy had left home for school on August 31 but did not return. Police said he was rescued from Azadpur Flyover on Friday after they chased the accused from Loni in Ghaziabad to Delhi, covering a distance of about 22 kilometres. The accused was fleeing by bus, police said.According to police, Pal wanted to marry the boy's sister and live with her, but she was unwilling to maintain any relationship with him.Police said the accused allegedly kidnapped her younger brother to pressure the family.He then called the boy's mother from an unknown number, identified himself and threatened to kill the child if his demand that the girl be sent to him was not fulfilled.The Jahangir Puri police station received a PCR call regarding the boy's disappearance on August 31 and registered an FIR based on the family's complaint.Officials said police developed leads regarding their movements through technical surveillance and field investigation and tracked them to Loni in Ghaziabad.(With inputs from PTI)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: 'Every corner of world but Bengal': State government's new tourism ad gets trolled
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The West Bengal government's state tourism ad was trolled by netizens after it failed to include anything that represents Bengal apart from.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The West Bengal government's state tourism ad was trolled by netizens after it failed to include anything that represents Bengal apart from the Howrah bridge.The ad was released on Friday by chief minister Suvendu Adhikari during a public event. "Hon'ble Chief Minister Shri Suvendu Adhikari attends the grand unveiling of West Bengal Tourism’s new brand identity, organized by the Department of Tourism, Government of West Bengal," the BJP state unit said posting video of the event.Though the ad begins with Howrah bridge, it progresses into showing Eiffel Tower, the Pyramids and several other world tourist attractions.TMC MP Derek O'Brien reacted to it calling it "Tacky. Trashy. Thooo.""Where is West Bengal in this?What kind of tourism logo reveal is this?? It is more like promoting international tourism rather than promoting Bengal! Everywhere but Bengal. Ridiculous," said a social media user Barnali Bairagi.Another user Joy said: "Let’s start with the bare minimum - The Background Music. With plethora of instruments available and tools to create OG music, they come with this trash that can put anyone to sleep (Play it on loop if u can’t sleep). The visuals and the shoddy video. It shows Howrah Bridge and moves on to deserts, pyramids, places that are not in West Bengal. Ya, the brilliant idea would have been to convey the experience of all the best things in the world u will find in West Bengal or something like that.""All they had to do is just study the communication and visual story telling of Kerala Tourism. Or even Odisha Tourism. Rajasthan Tourism also at one point of time had done great communications. The tagline: Where India feels different is so generic, it can be placed anywhere. It can even be the Tagline of an amusement park. Or a residential project. It doesn’t evoke any emotion. Compare it with Kerala tourism’s - God’s own Country. Or Rajasthan’s - Padharo Mhare Desh. Which is such a welcoming and warm tagline," the user added.Another user requested the CM to "ask the tourism department to create a fresh, professionally conceived, Bengal-centric campaign showcasing our mountains, forests, rivers, Sundarbans, coastline, heritage, literature, music, cuisine, festivals and extraordinary cultural diversity.""There was a time when Bengal Tourism meant Darjeeling, the Toy Train, Sundarbans, Howrah Bridge, trams, Jhau dance, heritage, culture and the unmistakable soul of Bengal. The “Sweetest Part of India” campaign showcased Bengal as Bengal," Diptangshu Chaudhury said."Bengal doesn’t need borrowed landmarks to attract the world. It needs the imagination and competence to showcase what it already has. From Darjeeling to the Sundarbans, from the Himalayas to the Bay of Bengal—Bengal itself is the advertisement. Please don’t make Bengal invisible while trying to sell it," the person added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Remains of 55 people recovered from Gaza rubble two years after strike
articles.summary: Civil defence officials in Gaza City said on Saturday that they have recovered the remains of 55 people from the rubble of a residential building destroyed i...
articles.body:
Civil defence officials in Gaza have recovered the remains of 55 people from a residential building destroyed in an Israeli airstrike two years ago.

The Gaza war, triggered by a massacre by Hamas and allied groups in 2023, has resulted in around 73,400 Palestinian deaths, with 82% of buildings in the Gaza Strip destroyed or damaged.

An estimated 10,000 to 14,000 people are still buried under rubble in Gaza, with a shortage of equipment hindering efforts to recover human remains from the aftermath of the conflict.

Civil defence officials in Gaza City said on Saturday that they have recovered the remains of 55 people from the rubble of a residential building destroyed in an Israeli airstrike two years ago.

Members of a family and numerous internally displaced persons had been staying in the house at the time, according to authorities conducting the clearance. Independent confirmation was not immediately available.

The Gaza war was triggered by the massacre by the Palestinian militant organization Hamas and allied groups on October 7, 2023. Around 200 people were killed in southern Israel and some 250 hostages were taken to the Gaza Strip.

According to the Hamas-controlled health authority in the coastal region, around 73,400 Palestinians have been killed since then. The figure does not differentiate between civilians and members of armed groups.

Eight out of 10 buildings destroyed or damaged

According to the United Nations Satellite Centre (UNOSAT), 82% of all buildings in the Gaza Strip were destroyed or damaged during the war.

Health authorities in Gaza, along with UN agencies and aid organizations, estimate that the remains of 10,000 to 14,000 people are still buried under rubble.

Civil defence authorities report an acute shortage of bulldozers, excavators and trucks to gain access to the missing and recover human remains.

Only a small portion of the more than 60 million tons of war debris has been cleared so far.

articles.title: H-1B petitions denied, visas revoked: USCIS says a 'major IT consulting' company in Vermont was doing this fraud
articles.summary: US News: As the Donald Trump administration intensified its crackdown on H-1B visa fraud, the US Citizenship and Immigration Services cited a specific case of .
articles.body: As the Donald Trump administration intensified its crackdown on H-1B visa fraud, the US Citizenship and Immigration Services cited a specific case of a major IT consulting company in Vermont that was giving lower salaries to H-1Bs. The agency said that it denied and revoked multiple petitions as such unfair practices hurt the interest of American workers."USCIS in Vermont identified H-1B petitions from a major IT consulting company that classified skilled technology jobs at wage levels below what the positions’ duties and requirements supported," the agency said."This practice undercuts required wages and creates unfair competition for US workers. We denied and revoked multiple petitions, protecting American workers and preserving the integrity of employment-based immigration programs," USCIS said.USCIS did not identify the consulting company involved. It also did not disclose how many H-1B petitions were affected or specify the technology positions that were examined. Social media users were, however, curious to know whether it was any of the major Indian IT companies.What did USCIS find?The latest action focuses on the wage level assigned to H-1B positions. Employers sponsoring foreign workers through the H-1B programme must comply with applicable wage requirements, and the wage classification associated with a position is tied to factors including the nature of the job, its requirements and the experience and skills expected from the worker.USCIS said the company had classified skilled technology positions at wage levels below what the agency determined was supported by the actual duties and requirements of those jobs.The agency's action means that the affected petitions have either been denied or revoked. A denial generally means a petition will not be approved, while revocation can affect a petition that had previously been approved.For an H-1B worker, the consequences of a revoked petition can depend on the circumstances of the case, including whether the worker has another valid immigration status or an alternative approved petition.What is an IT consulting company?An IT consulting company is a company that provides technology services to other businesses rather than primarily selling its own software or products. It can also refer to an IT staffing company which are called 'bodyshops' in Silicon Valley.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1844, a Mexican land grant gave settlers rights across what is now an 80,000-acre Colorado ranch; nearly two centuries later, the access fight has become the state’s longest-running land dispute
articles.summary: US News: A land dispute in Colorado dates back to an 1844 Mexican land grant and continues to involve questions over who can access the property and for what p.
articles.body: A land dispute in Colorado dates back to an 1844 Mexican land grant and continues to involve questions over who can access the property and for what purposes. The land, now known as Cielo Vista Ranch and traditionally called La Sierra, covers about 80,000 acres in Costilla County.According to the Colorado Governor’s Office, the Sangre de Cristo Land Grant was established in 1844 in connection with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo between the United States and Mexico. The property has since become the centre of a long-running legal dispute involving heirs of the original land grant and the owners of the ranch.The dispute has focused on access rights held by land grant heirs and community members. These rights include access for activities such as collecting firewood and grazing livestock. Over the years, landowners have restricted access to parts of the property, leading to repeated legal battles over the extent of those rights.The latest attempt to address the dispute came as Colorado Governor Jared Polis signed an executive order on Wednesday, naming former US Interior Secretary and Ambassador Ken Salazar as a special envoy. Salazar has been asked to help bring the different sides together and develop a recommendation on the long-term disagreements."We can and must do better than eternal litigation and conflict in our Colorado for all. This Executive Order is about creating an open dialogue, bringing together heirs of the original land grant, residents of the wider community and the property owner to find a path forward that improves quality of life in the valley. Coloradans in the San Luis Valley deserve a real seat at the table when it comes to decisions that shape our communities" Polis said in a statement.Salazar, meanwhie said, "I've spent my life in the San Luis Valley, and that's why I know how much this land means to the people who have called it home for generations. I'm looking forward to working alongside the community to listen closely, ask the right questions, and help find a path forward that works for all parties," he said.Decades-Old DisputeAccording to the Keystone Policy Center, the Cielo Vista Ranch/La Sierra dispute has been running for about 40 years, making it the longest-running legal dispute in Colorado. The organisation became involved after the new landowner and land grant heirs agreed in December 2018 to pause litigation and try to work through their differences.It facilitated meetings and discussions between the sides in an effort to find areas of common interest. The dispute, however, has continued through separate legal proceedings concerning access and the use of the property.A ruling reported in May 2026 also dealt with access for grazing. In that case, a special master, David Tenner, found that heirs could continue grazing sheep and cattle on La Sierra. At the same time, firewood gathering would end in a 233-acre area around the house.The ruling examined how people tending sheep could reach grazing areas. Testimony from sheep owners Alonzo Lobato and Richard Kuhn said handlers needed to pass through the disputed area to reach Perdido Canyon, an important grazing area.Tenner found that sheep required regular attention from the people looking after them. He also concluded that blocking access around the homesite would effectively prevent a reasonable route to Perdido Canyon.According to the ruling, older sheep trails had become overgrown during the prolonged dispute. A road built for the ranch owner's house about five years earlier had become the only workable route to the canyon. Tenner said the privacy area sought by the owner should be accompanied by an extended road or path that would allow access-rights holders to reach the canyon without going directly through the home area.A long historyThe Cielo Vista Ranch dispute is linked to the wider history of the Sangre de Cristo Land Grant. Keystone describes the 1844 grant as an 80,000-acre Mexican land grant along the Sangre de Cristo range and the only land grant of its kind in Colorado.The property is now privately owned, while heirs of the original land grant continue to assert historic access rights. The disagreements have included access for grazing and collecting firewood.In 2025, Polis signed HB 25-1023, a law providing local government oversight of large fencing projects on the Sangre de Cristo land grant. The law requires consideration of the environmental effects of such projects.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ‘Don’t give me these useless jumlas’: MP Kangana Ranaut pulls up officials over Rs 11 crore MPLADS funds
articles.summary: MANDI: BJP MP Kangana Ranaut pulled up officials during a DISHA Committee meeting in Himachal Pradesh over the alleged delay in implementing developme.
articles.body: MANDI: BJP MP Kangana Ranaut pulled up officials during a DISHA Committee meeting in Himachal Pradesh over the alleged delay in implementing development works under the Members of Parliament Local Area Development Scheme (MPLADS), questioning the utilisation of nearly Rs 11 crore allocated for projects in her constituency.Kangana expressed anger over what she described as repeated assurances from officials that there were no problems with the utilisation of MPLADS funds."Don’t give me these useless jumlas (fake promises). I’m getting them at every Disha Committee meeting. Last time as well, when I inquired about MPLADS, and our DISHA committees meet so regularly, whenever I asked about MPLADS, I was told that there was absolutely no hiccup and that 90% of our money was on the ground. But what turned out to be the reality? The reality came to light only when external agencies conducted detailed surveys on this..." she said."What I am trying to say is that I don't need your assurances to 'address' it—get the bloody job done now! The time for 'addressing' things is gone. Those are two-year-old matters. Those are one-and-a-half to two years old matters. Now get the job done and report to me that this is done!" she added.The BJP MP also questioned the utilisation of funds allocated for development works, saying nearly Rs 11 crore had been released while only a small portion had reportedly been spent. Reports said that in Mandi alone, around Rs 50-60 lakh had been utilised out of approximately Rs 5.5 crore.Ranaut further questioned the accountability and work ethic of officials, expressing concern over how she would explain the situation to the media and people of her constituency."What am I supposed to say before the media out there? That people come here only to draw their salaries? What am I supposed to say about the people of our state? What am I to say about their work ethic? That they are utterly lazy, utterly incompetent people occupying these chairs? Is that what I should say to the national media? About my own constituency? And about my own mountain people?..." she said.The MP directed officials to expedite the pending development works and report on their completion. Several projects have reportedly remained pending over issues including land availability and necessary permissions.(With Agency Inputs)Stay updated with the latest Shimla news. articles.body: ​Facebook-parent Meta is reportedly testing robots in its data centres. A report citing several current and former workers familiar with the projects noted that the social media giant is testing robots that can plug in cables, reset servers and take on other physical tasks inside its data centers.​A report by Wired cited Meta workers who wished to remain anonymous and said the company is using robots and related hardware from several different vendors, including Watney Robotics, Kinova and ABB. However, Meta and the robotics suppliers haven’t shared any official confirmation.​Meta's expanding use of robots could eventually let it run its rapidly growing data center footprint with fewer people, helping keep labour costs down even as its spending on AI infrastructure keeps climbing.​Meta testing robots for physical data center tasks​In one experiment, Meta is evaluating whether a Kinova Gen3 robotic arm could handle power cycling, or cutting off electricity to servers. The company is also testing a separate robot designed to swap networking cables, the report added.​One Meta data center worker estimates that if that effort succeeds, the bot could take over up to 80 per cent of some employees' workloads. "We thought those of us performing the physical tasks were safe for a while, but not anymore," the worker told Wired. "It's coming for us all, unfortunately."​At some facilities, Meta has quietly adopted a simpler device that resembles a finger, or a pointy stick, which can press the power button on a Mac Mini or other equipment to restart it remotely when prompted by a human.​In a statement, Meta spokesperson Francis Brennan said that the company is investing heavily in training and hiring workers to build and operate its data centers. "America is in the middle of its biggest infrastructure boom since World War II and there's a major shortage of skilled workers to fill the roles; we need more workers, not fewer," he said.​At a conference last year, Eric Xu, Meta's senior manager for robotics, said the company's long-term goals include putting robots in data centers, arguing they could speed up incident response, monitor conditions on site and handle preventative maintenance.​"We believe more collaboration and research will be needed, but we have to start otherwise we don't have a chance to do this," he said.Meta’s growing use of robots raises concerns over data center jobsMeta’s expansion of its use of robots in data centers is raising concerns among workers that automation could eventually replace some jobs or reduce the need for highly skilled employees. The company already uses robots to move server racks and track inventory, and to test machines for cabling, replace parts, and perform other maintenance tasks.Some robots still have limitations, including slow speeds, navigation problems, battery downtime, and difficulty reading equipment indicators, meaning humans remain necessary.Meta's Altoona, Iowa, data center is reportedly being used as a testing ground for newer robots, including dual-armed machines for cabling. The company is also testing robots at its New Albany, Ohio, campus, the report highlighted. However, robotics experts say there is still no proven solution capable of fully replacing humans in many data center tasks.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Remnants of Henry VIII's long-lost castle found in unexpected location, researcher reveals
articles.summary: Exclusive photos reveal pieces of King Henry VIII's lost Sandown Castle stonework traced to Dover Castle and Eastry Union Chapel across Kent, a researcher told Fox News Digital.
articles.body: Pieces of King Henry VIII's long-lost castle were recently found in a somewhat unexpected location: another English castle. The discovery by researcher Christopher Moore was recently announced by the University of Kent. Moore, who specializes in hidden and lost heritage, found evidence that stone used at Dover Castle was taken from Henry VIII's Sandown Castle, a Tudor coastal fortress built roughly 8 miles northeast of Dover that has since been lost to time. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER EERIE ANGLO-SAXON 'SAND BODIES' AT NUCLEAR POWER STATION SITE Built between 1539 and 1540 to defend the coast of England, Sandown was eventually abandoned and dismantled — and Moore found evidence that some of its stone was reused in a Victorian extension at Constable's Gate at Dover Castle. Moore traced the stone through historical records and architectural evidence, including an 1883 report documenting materials being sent from Sandown Castle to Dover. But Dover isn't the only place where pieces of Sandown found a second life. Moore has identified at least five sites where stone from the lost fortress was reused — and he singled out Eastry Union Chapel in Kent as perhaps the most interesting. ARCHAEOLOGISTS FIND ARTIFACTS OLDER THAN STONEHENGE BENEATH BRITAIN'S HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT: 'INCREDIBLY RARE' "It was built for a smaller budget than most of the other examples that I have found that were robbed from Sandown Castle," he told Fox News Digital. "Due to this, it contained the greatest variety of stonework, which is mainly 'freestones,' [or] stone that can be easily cut." Exclusive photographs shared with Fox News Digital show Eastry Union Chapel and its Sandown-linked patchwork of stonework. RARE 1,200-YEAR-OLD CHRISTIAN CROSS FOUND IN FIELD BY METAL DETECTORIST Moore added that most of the freestones probably came from ruined monasteries, some dating back to Norman England, hundreds of years before the Tudor period. "Even though Sandown is no longer standing, neither are many of the Norman monasteries that were spoiled to build these Tudor castles," he said. "Ancient buildings tell such great stories if only we learned to speak their language." "That's why Eastry Chapel is so exciting. It likely contains stonework that today has a near 1,000-year history." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Moore also took chemical samples from stone at Eastry and compared them with examples elsewhere in an effort to determine their origins. The time-consuming process created "a great web of where the masons were likely robbing the stone and where it was going," he noted. "Essentially, ancient buildings tell such great stories if only we learned to speak their language!" the researcher said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Moore believes many more examples of Sandown's reused masonry remain to be identified. "I know of at least five sites where stones were taken from Sandown for use elsewhere and [are] still standing today. However, there will be vastly more," Moore said. "Sandown did not just fall in the sea." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Moore has also contributed a chapter on Sandown Castle's forgotten history to the recently published book, "Revivalism in Architecture: Referencing and Reworking the Past." The researcher added that Tudor fortifications were built to be remarkably durable, pointing to Sandown's sister fortress, Deal Castle — which sustained relatively little damage to its original Tudor structure when it was struck by a bomb during World War II. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "For it to fall in the sea is a myth," added Moore. "[Sandown] was systematically robbed through the centuries for a number of uses."

articles.title: Ketan Agarwal murder: Friend of Chetan Choudhary held for conspiracy, 3rd arrest in case
articles.summary: PUNE: Pune Rural Police have arrested a 22-year-old man for allegedly being part of the conspiracy to kill realtor Ketan Agarwal at Lohagad Fort in Ju.
articles.body: PUNE: Pune Rural Police have arrested a 22-year-old man for allegedly being part of the conspiracy to kill realtor Ketan Agarwal at Lohagad Fort in June, making him the third accused to be held in the case, officials said on Saturday.The arrested man, Ritesh Hange, is a friend of Chetan Choudhary, who police allege was in a relationship with Agarwal's fiancée, Siya Goyal.Police said Goyal, 20, and Choudhary, 22, allegedly pushed Agarwal off a cliff at Lohagad Fort in Pune district on June 18, resulting in his death."During the investigation, it came to light that Ritesh was involved in the planning of Ketan Agarwal's murder," Pune Rural superintendent of police Sandip Singh Gill said.Hange has been arrested for his alleged role in the murder conspiracy, he said.Third arrest in Ketan Agarwal murder caseAnother police officer said Hange had been involved in planning the murder along with Choudhary and Goyal."He was aware of the earlier plan of Goyal and Chaudhary to injure Ketan by breaking his hands and legs and subsequently eliminate him. After allegedly executing the murder at Lohagad fort on June 18, Chetan contacted Ritesh and informed him about it," the officer said.Police said Hange was aware of the earlier plan to attack Agarwal before the alleged killing.Alleged love triangle behind realtor's killingAccording to police, Agarwal and Goyal had got engaged in February, while she was allegedly in a relationship with Choudhary.Investigators allege that Goyal and Choudhary planned to eliminate Agarwal as they considered him an obstacle in their relationship.Hange is the third person arrested in the case after Choudhary and Goyal.(With PTI inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Pune | Silver Rate in Pune | Bank Holidays in Pune | Public Holidays in Pune | Petrol Price in Pune | Diesel Price in Pune | CNG Price in Pune | LPG Price in PuneStay updated with the latest Pune news.
